content: 1. Vaginal discharge and undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding should be evaluated thoroughly to determine the underlying cause. 2. Estrogen therapy is contraindicated in individuals with a known, suspected, or history of breast cancer or estrogen-dependent neoplasia. 3. Active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or a history of these conditions are contraindications for estrogen use. 4. Active arterial thromboembolic disease, such as stroke or myocardial infarction (MI), or a history of these conditions, precludes the use of estrogen therapy. 5. Estrogen should not be used in individuals with a known anaphylactic reaction or angioedema caused by estrogen. 6. Estrogen therapy is contraindicated in patients with known liver impairment or disease. 7. Individuals with known deficiencies in protein C, protein S, antithrombin, or other thrombophilic disorders should avoid estrogen therapy. 8. Estrogen therapy is not recommended in known or suspected pregnancy. 9. Systemic absorption occurs with intravaginal administration of estrogen; therefore, warnings, precautions, and adverse effects associated with systemic estrogen-alone therapy should be considered. 10. Estrogen-alone therapy has been associated with an increased risk of stroke and DVT, while estrogen plus progestin therapy has been linked to an increased risk of PE, DVT, stroke, and MI. Discontinue the drug immediately if these conditions occur or are suspected. 11. The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin substudy reported a statistically nonsignificant increased risk of ovarian cancer. 12. Estrogen, with or without progesterone, may increase the risk of dementia in postmenopausal women. 13. Postmenopausal women receiving estrogen therapy have a 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. 14. Severe hypercalcemia has been reported in women with breast cancer and bone metastases using estrogen. If hypercalcemia occurs, discontinue estrogen and initiate appropriate treatment to reduce serum calcium levels. 15. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported with estrogen use. Discontinue estrogen pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia, or migraine. Permanently discontinue estrogen if papilledema or retinal vascular lesions are diagnosed. 16. Rare cases of substantial blood pressure increases due to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogen have been reported. 17. Estrogen may elevate triglyceride levels, potentially leading to pancreatitis in women with preexisting hypertriglyceridemia. Discontinue estrogen if pancreatitis occurs. 18. Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in individuals with hepatic impairment. If cholestatic jaundice occurs, discontinue estrogen therapy. Exercise caution in women with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or pregnancy. 19. Estrogen administration increases thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels. Women with normal thyroid function can compensate by producing more thyroid hormone, maintaining normal free T4 and T3 levels. However, women dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy may require increased doses of their thyroid medication. Monitor thyroid function in these women during treatment. 20. Estrogens may cause fluid retention. Women with conditions that could be influenced by fluid retention, such as cardiac or renal impairment, should be carefully monitored. Discontinue estrogen-alone therapy if medically concerning fluid retention occurs. 21. Malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants has been reported in women treated with estrogen-alone therapy post-hysterectomy. If residual endometriosis exists, consider adding progestin. 22. Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of angioedema in women with hereditary angioedema. Weigh the benefits and risks of estrogen therapy in such cases. 23. Estrogen therapy may worsen conditions such as asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. Assess whether the benefits of estrogen therapy outweigh the risks in women with these conditions. 24. Local abrasions caused by vaginal tablet applicators have been reported. 25. Serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and estradiol levels are not shown to be effective for managing moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause. 26. Estrogen therapy may alter coagulation parameters, including increased prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and platelet aggregation time, as well as increased levels of clotting factors and fibrinogen. 27. Estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur in women with hypoparathyroidism. Consider the risks and benefits of estrogen therapy in such cases. 28. Estrogen therapy is not indicated for use during pregnancy. Epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have not shown an increased risk of birth defects following exposure to combined hormonal contraceptives before conception or during early pregnancy. 29. Estrogens are present in human milk and may reduce milk production in breastfeeding women. This reduction is less likely once breastfeeding is well-established. Consider the clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. 30. Exogenous estrogens are metabolized similarly to endogenous estrogens, undergoing enterohepatic recirculation and metabolic interconversions primarily in the liver. 31. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be converted to estriol, the major urinary metabolite. 32. In postmenopausal women, a significant portion of circulating estrogens exists as sulfate conjugates, particularly estrone sulfate, which serves as a reservoir for the formation of more active estrogens. 33. Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine along with glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. 34. Estrogens, whether used alone or with progestin, have rarely caused serious side effects. Discuss the risks and benefits of hormone treatment with your doctor. 35. Estrogens can increase the risk of uterine cancer (endometrial cancer). Taking progestin as directed by your doctor can help reduce this risk. 36. In postmenopausal women, estrogens, taken with or without progestin, increase the risk of breast/ovarian cancer, stroke, dementia, and serious blood clots. 37. The risk of serious side effects may depend on the dose of estrogen and the duration of use. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time necessary. 38. Regular physical exams, including blood pressure checks, breast exams/mammograms, pelvic exams, and Pap smears, should be conducted while using this medication. 39. Preventing or controlling high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes can reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke. Lifestyle changes such as reducing stress, eating a low-fat/salt diet, losing weight, exercising regularly, and quitting smoking can help. 40. Keep your mind active with mental exercises to help prevent dementia. 41. Store the medication at room temperature and discard it properly when expired or no longer needed. 42. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
